package_info.package_manager: Microsoft Office (macro-enabled Word document, distributed via ISO archive)
package_info.why_malicious: The document is weaponized with a multi-stage macro that delivers a backdoor (Havoc Demon agent) to the victim's system. It uses obfuscated VBA macros, anti-analysis techniques, and custom payload storage to evade detection, ultimately granting remote control to the attacker.

execution_context.file_location: VBA macro in Word document (EbDYTPZ.vEypm, referenced in document.xml.rels)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
For Each s In ActiveDocument.Shapes
  If s.Name = "happy" Then s.Delete
Next
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code iterates through all Shape objects in the document, deletes the one named 'happy', and removes the overlay image to simulate revealing protected content, deceiving the user into enabling further macro execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code manipulates document content to deceive the user into believing protected information has been revealed, which is a common social engineering tactic to encourage macro enablement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal macros should not manipulate document overlays to trick users into enabling further execution or to simulate document unlocking.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate macros may remove overlays for document formatting or template purposes, but not as part of a social engineering lure to enable malicious actions.
key_indicators: Deletes overlay image upon macro enablement
Removes visual block to simulate document unlocking

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
If Dir("C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll") <> "" Then
  ShellExecute ...
Else
  ' Extract payload from custom XML part
End If
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code checks for the existence of a hardcoded DLL path in the user's AppData directory; if present, it executes the DLL, otherwise it proceeds to extract and decode a payload from the document's custom XML part, enabling staged payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Checking for and executing a DLL from a hardcoded path in the user's AppData directory is a strong indicator of persistence or staged malware delivery, and is not typical for legitimate Office macros.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not execute binaries from user directories or check for malware persistence mechanisms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, enterprise macros may check for helper DLLs, but not in this context and not with hardcoded paths in user directories.
key_indicators: Staged payload logic based on file presence

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
For Each part In ActiveDocument.CustomXMLParts
  If part.SelectSingleNode("//TwXfx") Is Not Nothing Then
    payload = part.SelectSingleNode("//TwXfx").Text
    ' Base64 decode, add 35, xor 82
  End If
Next
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code enumerates custom XML parts in the document, locates the node 'TwXfx', extracts its content, decodes it using Base64 followed by custom arithmetic and XOR operations, and reconstructs the binary payload for later execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Storing and extracting a binary payload from custom XML parts is a stealthy technique to evade static detection and hide malicious content within document metadata.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal macros do not store or reconstruct executables from document XML data, nor do they use custom encoding/decoding logic.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Custom XML parts are used for document metadata or configuration, not for storing encoded binaries or payloads.
key_indicators: Custom XML node with encoded binary ('TwXfx')

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
Open "C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll" For Binary As #1
Put #1, , decoded_payload
Close #1
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code writes the decoded payload to a hardcoded DLL path in the user's AppData directory, persisting the malicious binary to disk for subsequent execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Writing an executable to a user directory is a classic malware dropper behavior, especially when using misleading filenames to masquerade as legitimate Office components.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate macros should not write arbitrary binaries to disk, particularly in locations associated with trusted software.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may write DLLs, but not via Office macros and not to user-specific Office directories.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At document-open, the code launches the dropped payload by executing conhost.exe in headless mode with the path to the malicious DLL, initiating the next stage of the attack chain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching a dropped DLL via conhost.exe is a process injection and evasion technique, leveraging a legitimate system process to execute malicious code in a less conspicuous manner.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Macros should not launch system processes to execute arbitrary DLLs, especially using headless or hidden execution modes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare in legitimate automation; not typically performed by user macros or document automation.
key_indicators: Abuse of conhost.exe for DLL execution
Headless execution to avoid user detection
Direct execution of recently dropped DLL

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Read .vdata section
If RC4-encrypted, decrypt with key
If LZNT1-compressed, decompress
Parse loader config
Inject shellcode into current or new process using ZwCreateThreadEx with THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At payload execution, the loader reads the .vdata section, decrypts it with RC4 if encrypted, decompresses with LZNT1 if compressed, parses the loader configuration, and injects the next-stage shellcode into memory using ZwCreateThreadEx with anti-debugging flags, enabling stealthy in-memory execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Custom in-memory unpacking, process injection, and use of anti-debugging thread creation flags are hallmarks of advanced malware loaders designed to evade analysis and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate DLLs do not inject shellcode or manipulate thread creation flags for stealth or anti-debugging purposes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team tools and some security products may use similar techniques, but not in userland Office DLLs or in this context.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Locate PE headers in memory (0x4d 0x5a, 0x50 0x45)
Resolve LdrLoadDll, NtAllocateVirtualMemory, NtProtectVirtualMemory via API hashing
Allocate memory, load Demon agent DLL, execute in memory
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At payload execution, the shellcode locates the embedded Demon agent DLL in memory by searching for PE headers, resolves necessary APIs using hashing, allocates memory, and loads and executes the agent directly from memory, avoiding disk writes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: In-memory DLL loading and API hashing are advanced evasion and anti-analysis techniques that allow malware to execute without leaving artifacts on disk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal code does not perform in-memory PE parsing and API resolution via hashes, especially not in the context of Office document execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team frameworks and some security tools use similar methods for in-memory execution, but not in userland Office document scenarios.
key_indicators: No disk artifacts for loaded agent

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
// Pseudocode
Generate random 256-bit key and 128-bit IV
Send HTTP/HTTPS POST to ukrtatnafta[.]org with check-in data (agent ID, command ID, AES key/IV, encrypted data)
Receive and execute C2 commands (enumerate system, execute commands, inject code, manipulate files, take screenshots, etc.)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the Demon agent generates a random 256-bit key and 128-bit IV, sends an HTTP/HTTPS POST request to the hardcoded C2 domain ukrtatnafta[.]org with check-in data (including agent ID, command ID, AES key/IV, and encrypted data), and receives and executes attacker commands such as system enumeration, command execution, code injection, file manipulation, and screenshot capture, enabling full remote control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: C2 communication, system enumeration, and remote command execution are core backdoor behaviors, and the use of AES-encrypted traffic to a hardcoded domain is a strong indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate DLL should establish covert C2 channels, exfiltrate data, or enable remote control over the system.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red-team agents and penetration testing tools may use similar techniques, but not in production or user environments.
key_indicators: Wide range of post-exploitation features (system enumeration, command execution, file manipulation, screenshot capture)

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious document and enables macros, triggering macro execution that manipulates document content and checks for existing payload.
Macro checks for existing payload, and if not present, extracts and decodes binary from custom XML part, reconstructing the payload.
Macro launches the dropped payload (OfficeTelemetry.dll) using conhost.exe in headless mode, initiating execution of the loader.
Loader (OfficeTelemetry.dll) unpacks, decrypts, and injects shellcode into memory using anti-debugging and stealth techniques.
Shellcode (KaynLdr) locates and loads Demon agent DLL in memory, resolving APIs via hashing and executing the agent without writing to disk.
Demon agent establishes encrypted C2 channel to ukrtatnafta[.]org, receives and executes attacker commands for full remote control.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control of victim system

behavioral_signatures: Office macro extracting and decoding binary payloads from custom XML parts using non-standard node names and custom decoding logic
Macros writing executables (DLLs) to user AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office directories with misleading filenames
Macros launching DLLs via conhost.exe or similar system processes in headless mode
In-memory unpacking and injection of shellcode using ZwCreateThreadEx with THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER
Network connections to hardcoded C2 domains (e.g., ukrtatnafta[.]org) with custom HTTP headers and AES-encrypted payloads
Macros or payloads that enumerate system information, execute arbitrary commands, or manipulate files post-infection
file_indicators: Word documents with non-standard macro storage (e.g., EbDYTPZ.vEypm instead of vbaProject.bin)
Presence of OfficeTelemetry.dll in user AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office
Custom XML parts with node names like TwXfx containing Base64-encoded and custom-encoded data
network_indicators: Connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and related subpaths (e.g., /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/avias.js)
HTTP/HTTPS POST requests with headers mimicking legitimate web traffic (e.g., Content-Type: application/javascript, User-Agent: Chrome/108.0.0.0)
AES-encrypted payloads in POST data to non-standard endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents with macros that access custom XML parts and write executables to disk, especially in AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office. Flag any macro that writes to OfficeTelemetry.dll or launches DLLs via conhost.exe in headless mode. Detect in-memory unpacking and process injection behaviors, particularly those using ZwCreateThreadEx with anti-debugging flags. Monitor outbound network traffic for connections to ukrtatnafta[.]org and similar domains, especially with suspicious HTTP headers and encrypted payloads. Use YARA rules to identify custom XML nodes (e.g., TwXfx) containing Base64-encoded or custom-encoded data in Office documents. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators for high-confidence detection.
